Capital One. What's in your wallet? Terms apply. Details at CapitalOne.com.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Amy Held. The FAA is examining what caused Friday's ground
stop that is still disrupting flights more than 5,000 so far today. NPR's Eva Berger reports
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is blaming a contractor's work on outdated technology for the
meltdown. NPR reached out for comment from L3 Harris. In a public statement, the company said
that it has been working with the FAA to convert those old wires to a fiber optic system. And it
says it has completed more than 70% of those conversions. L3 Harris said it is supporting the
FAA in their investigation. In a video on the company's website, L3 Harris touts the work the
company is doing to update the FAA's communication systems. The brand new air traffic control system
will enhance safety, reduce delays, and pave the way for new technologies like flying taxis and
drones. The website also says its FAA telecom infrastructure supports 45,000 daily flights.
Eva Berger, NPR News, Washington. President Trump heads to Asia tomorrow. First up is Manila
for the ASEAN Summit. That's the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Security and Trade are
on the agenda. Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of
Notre Dame, says the summit is strategically important. The phrase Southeast Asia was actually
coined by U.S. military planners as part of a counterweight to thinking about the geopolitical
dimensions of East Asia, where historically the People's Republic of China has been dominant.
It has allies and democracy. It has military bases. It also has very strategic maritime waterways.
Wednesday, Trump is set to visit China for a historic three-way meeting with President Xi Jinping
and Vladimir Putin of Russia to talk about their nuclear stockpiles. In Bahrain, overnight,
Iranian forces said they launched a retaliatory attack on a U.S. radar system at an airbase,
the second such attack since Friday. NPR's Aya Batrawi reports. Iran's state media reported
the sound of explosions in Iranian territory near the Strait of Hormuz after midnight Sunday,
without elaborating further. Soon after, Iran's Revolutionary Guard issued a statement
saying it had delivered a "crushing response" to U.S. military aggression by launching six
drones targeting a U.S. radar in Bahrain. It said it launched this number of drones
to ensure the U.S. understands any act of aggression will be met with a severe response.
Bahrain confirmed the Iranian attack, saying its air defenses intercepted them all.
U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment.
The apparent tit-for-tat attacks come as Iran continues attacking oil tankers in the Strait of
Hormuz, including it says two on Sunday with mines. Aya Batrawi, NPR News, Dubai.
It's NPR News.
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park in
Washington. President Trump said the municipal golf course and park would shut today ahead of
renovation work. It's the latest setback to his renovation projects around the Capitol.
Food-laden holiday dinners and parties will be taking place over the next two months.
The Environmental Protection Agency says the average American household
wastes nearly $3,000 a year on uneaten food. Scott Massione from member station WYPR has this report.
The U.S. wastes about 30 percent of the food supply, and half of that comes from households,
according to Johns Hopkins environmental health researcher Ronnie Neff.
But there are ways to get some of that back.
Use your freezer. There's a lot of things that can be frozen that, you know,
most people don't recognize. Neff says to remember to label those foods and consider
having a day for eating leftover meals each week to ensure everything gets gobbled up.
Another way to reduce waste is using online food calculators to make portions suitable
for the number of guests at a party. For NPR News, I'm Scott Massione in Baltimore.
An art world mystery buried behind coats and boxes has come to light. A Manhattan woman had
kept a Georgia O'Keeffe painting in her apartment closet for decades. She died recently in her 90s,
and now the artwork of a New Mexico landscape is going up for auction Tuesday.
It's estimated to be worth millions. Last known to have been sold in 1963 for $3,800,
O'Keeffe, known as the mother of American modernism, is celebrated for her abstract
paintings of flowers and of the Southwest. You're listening to NPR News.
This message comes from Cure Alzheimer's Fund. From family to community,
connections and the memories they make are everything. The hugs, the strolls, the laughs,
songs, and dreams. Cure Alzheimer's Fund empowers the scientists who dedicate their lives to curing
Alzheimer's disease. Great progress has been made, and the momentum is building. There is more to do.
Learn more at curealz.org. Let's keep our memories together.
